title: Dinosaur-killing impact crater might have been teeming with life
gist: Potassium-argon dating of feldspar drilled from the Chicxulub crater, combined with simulations, shows its impact-driven hydrothermal system lasted about 8 million years (66 to 58 Ma), four times longer than the previous estimate of 2 million years. That would have left a long window for microbial life. The study does not show that the system was actually inhabited. The piece is pure science with little direct investor relevance.

insights.claim: Simulations indicate the Chicxulub system took 1.5 to 2.3 million years to cool to 90°C at 1 km depth and up to 5 million years to fall below 50°C. Flow dropped sharply after 6 million years and stopped by 8 million, consistent with the isotope ages.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Rayne
insights.so_what: Two independent methods agree, which strengthens confidence in the finding.

insights.claim: Pickersgill argues that longer hydrothermal activity widens the window for prebiotic chemistry, the origin of life, and the spread of microorganisms.

insights.claim: Pickersgill suggests that impacts larger than Chicxulub, on early Earth or other planetary bodies, could have produced even longer-lived hydrothermal systems that stayed habitable for at least several million years.
